poteto-mode.one: The router. Matches your request to a playbook and runs it.
poteto-mode.when: Any non-trivial task. This is the default entry point and usually the only thing you type.
poteto-mode.use: Describe the work in plain words, including how you want it proven. It picks the playbook, copies its steps into your task list verbatim, and delegates. It is sticky: it stays on across turns until you say `pstack off`.
poteto-mode.pitfall: Reaching past it for a named skill. The router already calls `/how`, `/architect`, `/interrogate` and the rest when a step needs them; calling one yourself skips the playbook that would have sequenced it.

setup-pstack.one: Detects your host, probes what it can really do, writes the config.
setup-pstack.when: Once per project, before anything else. Again if skills degrade unexpectedly or you change models.
setup-pstack.use: Run it and answer the questions. It writes `.pstack/host.json` (capabilities, tier) and `.pstack/models.md` (role to model). Both override the build-time defaults.
setup-pstack.pitfall: Skipping it. Without it pstack runs on build-time guesses about your host rather than what your session can actually do.

how.one: Explains how a subsystem works, at senior-onboarding depth.
how.when: Before changing unfamiliar code. Also for placement questions: where should this live, which package owns it, is this the right layer.
how.use: Ask the real question. For a wide subsystem it fans out explorers on separate angles then synthesizes; for a narrow one it answers in a single pass. Output is Overview, Key Concepts, How It Works, Where Things Live, Gotchas.
how.pitfall: Using it for motivation. `/how` is runtime behaviour; `/why` is intent. Asking `/how` why a threshold is 750ms gets you the mechanism, not the reason.

why.one: Finds the intent behind code, cited.
why.when: A decision looks wrong and you suspect it is not. Regressions, postmortems, data-backed thresholds, 'why did we pick Y'.
why.use: It discovers the evidence sources available to you and queries them in parallel: source control, issue tracker, long-form docs, chat, observability, error tracking, analytics. Returns a cited read with a Sources Consulted block.
why.pitfall: Trusting an uncited claim. If a tool server was unreachable the skill says so; that gap is the finding, not a detail to skim.

teach.one: Runs `/how` and `/why` and weaves one plain explanation.
teach.when: You want to genuinely understand a subsystem or a change, not just get past it.
teach.use: Name the thing and your current level. It combines mechanism and history at your pace.
teach.pitfall: Using it when you only need one half. It costs two investigations.

recall.one: Rebuilds your recent context on a topic from your own history.
recall.when: Starting your day, resuming after a break, or taking over work you half-remember.
recall.use: Name the topic. It mines your recent sessions and the shared record and hands back a tight current-state brief: where things stand, what is verified, what is open.
recall.pitfall: Expecting it where the host keeps no readable transcripts. It will say so and rebuild from the repo instead, which is weaker.

architect.one: Settles types, signatures and module shape before any implementation.
architect.when: Code that crosses a function boundary. Anything where jumping straight to code would lock in the wrong shape.
architect.use: Phases: Ground the problem, Sketch (signatures with `not implemented` bodies), Agree (optional checkpoint with you), Implement against the sketch, Scrap if the architecture turns out wrong. Read the sketch before it implements.
architect.pitfall: Treating the sketch as binding. Phase E exists because sketches are sometimes wrong; scrapping one early is cheaper than implementing it.

arena.one: N parallel attempts at the same task, pick a base, graft the best of the rest.
arena.when: One attempt would lock in the wrong shape and the design space is genuinely open.
arena.use: Frame the rubric first, since candidates only see the task. It fans out, cross-judges on a different model family, picks a base, then grafts. Read the synthesis note: it records what was grafted and what was rejected.
arena.pitfall: Running it where the answer is knowable. If a prototype could settle it by observation, that is cheaper and more conclusive.

swarm.one: N parallel workers over separate slices or racing the same brief.
swarm.when: Coverage matrices, races, gauntlets, wide exploration. Work that partitions cleanly.
swarm.use: Frame the slices, fan out, the parent waits and aggregates into one report. Use it for breadth; use `/arena` when you want competing designs of the same thing.
swarm.pitfall: Slices that share state. Give each worker its own directory or worktree, or they will overwrite each other.

interrogate.one: Several reviewers try to break your diff from independent angles.
interrogate.when: A contested design, or a diff you do not trust, before it ships.
interrogate.use: Give it the diff and state the intent. Reviewers work blind to each other; the lead synthesizes and gives a judgment. Where your host has one model family it uses adversarial stances instead and says so.
interrogate.pitfall: Reading agreement as safety. Agreement between two passes of one model is not evidence; the output tells you which you got.

blast-radius.one: What else this change could break, proven by running code.
blast-radius.when: A small-looking change you do not fully trust. Reviewing someone else's diff.
blast-radius.use: It looks beyond the diff and then proves the one fact the change is safe because of, by running something rather than asserting it.
blast-radius.pitfall: Accepting a writeup. The skill's own first rule is not to trust its own writeup; the evidence is the run.

no-comments.one: Deletes narrating comments and fixes the code they were hiding.
no-comments.use: It delegates to `comment-sicko`, which is deliberately hostile to comments, then you act on accepted findings. A comment claiming a constraint gets offered as a type, test or lint instead.
no-comments.pitfall: Letting it strip a comment that encodes a real external constraint. Legal headers, public API docs, and vendor-forced behaviour survive; check the rejects.

unslop.when: Any prose surface: replies, docs, PR bodies, commit messages. The router applies it automatically.
unslop.use: Point it at the text. It removes the long-dash habit, filler, jargon, and the communication artifacts that make writing read as generated.
unslop.pitfall: Expecting it to clean code. It is prose only; `/no-comments` handles code.

technical-writing.one: Four-layer standard for docs a tired engineer understands first read.
technical-writing.when: Docs, RFCs, readmes, PR descriptions, commit messages.
technical-writing.use: Pick the Diatax is mode first, then Google developer style for sentences, STE rules so statements land one at a time, Global English so no sentence has two readings.
technical-writing.pitfall: Applying all four layers to a two-line commit message. Match the layer count to the surface.

tdd.one: Makes the broken behaviour executable before you change production code.
tdd.when: A bug with a clear, cheap test path. Only when asked, or when the target is obvious.
tdd.use: Write the failing test, then fix. Stage commits so the failing repro lands before the fix in history.
tdd.pitfall: Forcing it. The skill itself says to skip when the test path is unclear, expensive or integration-heavy.

figure-it-out.one: Designs a bespoke playbook when none of the 23 fits.
figure-it-out.when: A large migration, an ambitious multi-part change, or work you will review after stepping away.
figure-it-out.use: The deliverable before any code is the workflow itself. It frames, designs phases, runs a hypothesis loop, keeps an audit trail, then verifies.
figure-it-out.pitfall: Using it when a narrower playbook fits. Bespoke costs more and proves less than a playbook that has been run many times.

create-verification-skill.one: Generates a project-local way to drive your real app and prove behaviour.
create-verification-skill.when: Your repo has no scripted way to launch the app, exercise a feature and capture evidence.
create-verification-skill.use: It interviews the repo rather than you, generates the skill, seeds a feature map, then proves the generated skill before handing it over.
create-verification-skill.pitfall: Skipping it and letting 'it compiles' stand in for proof. Most of pstack's verification steps assume this exists.

maintain-verification-skill.one: The upkeep loop for a generated verification skill.
maintain-verification-skill.when: Periodically, or when the feature map has drifted from the app.
maintain-verification-skill.use: Parallel source readers per feature, one live session driving every feature, at most one PR of proven corrections.
maintain-verification-skill.pitfall: Letting the map rot. A stale feature map makes every verification step quietly weaker.

show-me-your-work.one: A reviewable decision trail, one row per decision.
show-me-your-work.when: Long-running or unattended work, or anything you will review after stepping away.
show-me-your-work.use: A TSV with what, why, evidence, result. Local by default; commit it when a reviewer needs the trail to trust the result. It audits itself against the transcript at the end.
show-me-your-work.pitfall: Writing it at the end. A trail reconstructed afterwards records what you remember, not what happened.

reflect.one: Mines the session for learnings and routes each into a skill edit.
reflect.when: After a session that taught you something about how the agent should work.
reflect.use: Three reviewers in parallel over the transcript, then a synthesizer that returns Accepted, Rejected and Backlog. Accepted items become concrete edits.
reflect.pitfall: Running it on a routine session. Without real friction to mine, it produces noise.

automate-me.one: Builds a personal mode skill from your own working history.
automate-me.when: You want agents to follow how you actually work without describing it.
automate-me.use: It mines recent transcripts for repeated preferences, asks which patterns are really you, drafts a `-mode` skill, unslops it, and opens a PR.
automate-me.pitfall: Accepting every mined pattern. It asks for a reason: some habits are accidents, not preferences.

make-bot-ui.one: A page you click that wakes an agent over a trigger.
make-bot-ui.when: You want a dashboard or buttons that start agent work.
make-bot-ui.use: A local server holds the key and POSTs to the trigger; the browser never sees the key. Bind to 0.0.0.0 and expose over Tailscale. Treat the incoming body as untrusted data.
make-bot-ui.pitfall: Putting the sender key in the browser or in chat. That publishes it.

bro.one: Restates the last message in plain language.
bro.when: An answer was dense or jargon-heavy.

typescript-best-practices.one: TypeScript patterns, applied automatically on .ts and .tsx files.
typescript-best-practices.when: Automatic. It attaches when you touch matching files.
typescript-best-practices.use: Nothing to invoke. It builds on the type-system-discipline principle.
typescript-best-practices.pitfall: Assuming it covers design. It covers types; `/architect` covers shape.
